cards.front: What does a pyramid-shaped age structure diagram with a wide base predict about a population?
cards.back: **Rapid growth**, because a very large pre-reproductive group will soon enter the reproductive years and have children.
cards.hint: Look at which age group is largest at the bottom of the diagram.

cards.front: Why is the size of the pre-reproductive group a key clue to future growth?
cards.back: Those **children** will soon enter the reproductive group and have children of their own, so future births are likely to rise.
cards.hint: Follow the young people forward through the age groups over time.

cards.back: Continued **population growth** after birth rates fall, because a large pre-reproductive group is moving into the reproductive years.

cards.front: What is an age structure diagram?
cards.back: A **bar graph** showing how many individuals, or what percent, fall in each age group, with the youngest group at the bottom.

cards.front: Which ages make up the reproductive group?
cards.back: Ages **15 to 44**, when most births occur.
cards.hint: Compare with the pre-reproductive group, which covers the younger ages.

cards.front: Which ages make up the post-reproductive group?
cards.back: Ages **45 and older**, when few births occur.

cards.front: Why is a narrow base not proof that a population is already shrinking?
cards.back: A narrow base predicts **future decline**, because smaller groups will replace larger ones. The population may not be shrinking yet.
cards.hint: Think about what the age groups will do over time, not only what they are now.

cards.front: Why does a large post-reproductive group point toward decline?
cards.back: Deaths rise while births stay low, so there are fewer young people to replace the older generation.
cards.hint: Consider how many people in this group are still having children.

cards.front: Why can an age structure diagram not give an exact future population size?
cards.back: **Migration** and later changes in birth and death rates also change population size, and the diagram shows only current age groups.
cards.hint: Think about what the diagram does not show.

cards.front: A country has $14$ million people aged 0 to 14, $22$ million aged 15 to 44 and $4$ million aged 45 or older. What percent are aged 15 to 44?
What formula gives the percent share of an age group in a population?
cards.hint: Think about dividing a part by the whole.

cards.front: What should you check if your three age group percentages do not add to 100%?
cards.back: Recheck the **total population**, because the shares should always sum to 100%.
cards.hint: Work backwards from the total you added up.

cards.front: What steps should you follow when predicting a population's trend from its age structure?
cards.back: Name the **largest group**, say what it will do over the next 20 years, then state the trend: growth, steady or decline.
cards.hint: Start with the group that stands out most on the diagram.

cards.front: Which age structure shape predicts stable or slow growth?
cards.back: A **straight-sided column**, where the pre-reproductive group is similar in size to the other groups.
cards.hint: Compare the width of the base with the width of the rest of the bars.
